questions.question: For a real-valued function $f\colon\boldsymbol{E}\to\mathbb{R}$ with $\boldsymbol{E}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, what is $\nabla f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)$?
options: The matrix of second partial derivatives at $\boldsymbol{x}_0$.
The scalar sum of the first partial derivatives at $\boldsymbol{x}_0$.
The column vector of first partial derivatives at $\boldsymbol{x}_0$.

questions.question: What condition on $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ is included for the gradient?
options: $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ is a boundary point of the set $\boldsymbol{E}$.

questions.question: Let $f\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $\boldsymbol{x}_0$, and let $\boldsymbol{v}$ be a unit vector. What does $\nabla f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\cdot\boldsymbol{v}$ represent in general?
options: The steepest rate of increase of $f$ at $\boldsymbol{x}_0$.

questions.question: Why does the definition require $f$ to be real-valued?
options: Because partial derivatives exist only for functions into $\mathbb{R}$.
Because only real-valued functions can be totally differentiable.
Because the gradient is the vector of partial derivatives of one scalar function.
Because a real-valued $f$ is guaranteed to have all of its first partial derivatives.

questions.question: For $f(x,y) = \mathrm{e}^{x+y}$, at which point below is the gradient equal to $\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$?

Let $f$ be totally differentiable at $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ with $\nabla f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\neq\boldsymbol{0}$. Which claim about the directional derivatives $\mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{v}}f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)$ over unit vectors $\boldsymbol{v}$ is justified?
options: They take the same value for every unit vector $\boldsymbol{v}$.
The largest value is attained when $\boldsymbol{v}$ points along $\nabla f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)$.
They are zero when $\boldsymbol{v}$ points along $\nabla f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)$, as the gradient is tangent to the level curve.
The most negative value is attained when $\boldsymbol{v}$ points along $\nabla f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)$.

questions.question: Let $f$ be totally differentiable at $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ with $\nabla f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)=\begin{pmatrix}3\\4\end{pmatrix}$, and let $\boldsymbol{v}=\begin{pmatrix}3/5\\4/5\end{pmatrix}$. What is $\mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{v}}f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)$?
Let $E\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ and $f\colon E\to\mathbb{R}$. How many components does $\nabla f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)$ have?
options: $n$ components, one for each input variable.
$n^2$ components, one for each pair of input variables.
$n+1$ components: the $n$ partial derivatives together with $f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)$.

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ be an interior point of the domain of $f$ at which $\nabla f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)=\boldsymbol{0}$. Which conclusion is justified?
options: $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ is a stationary point of $f$, which need not be a local extremum.
$\boldsymbol{x}_0$ is a local extremum point of $f$, since the gradient vanishes only at extrema.
$f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)=0$, since all the partial derivatives of $f$ vanish there.
$f$ is constant on some open ball around $\boldsymbol{x}_0$, since its rate of change there is $0$.

questions.question: Suppose all first partial derivatives of $f$ exist at the interior point $\boldsymbol{x}_0$, so $\nabla f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)$ is defined. Which assumption guarantees $\nabla f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\cdot\boldsymbol{v}=\mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{v}}f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)$ for every unit vector $\boldsymbol{v}$?
options: None: the existence of all first partial derivatives already guarantees it.
